claim: Path E reframes the toxicity-prediction direction halted at Gate B (Session 22) as a saturating-inhibitor analysis on already-computed v15 single-knockout predictions. Treats compound that fully inhibits enzyme X as equivalent to knockout of gene X — bypasses the need to extend Layer 2 with kinetic inhibition rate laws. Identifies 6 SBML-encoded enzymes that ARE canonical antibiotic drug targets (contradicting Gate B's '0 of 155' claim, which was triggered by a too-narrow regex pattern in the Session-22 notebook): JCVISYN3A_0519 (ileRS / mupirocin target), JCVISYN3A_0634 (leuRS / tavaborole target), JCVISYN3A_0012 (metRS / REP3123 target), JCVISYN3A_0045 (tmk / dTMP-kinase nucleoside-analog target), JCVISYN3A_0076 (asnRS / tirandamycin-family target), JCVISYN3A_0819 (trxB thioredoxin-disulfide reductase / auranofin target). All six are v15-essential AND Breuer-essential. The Path E saturating-inhibitor verdict is CONSISTENT for all six — the simulator predicts cell death under saturating inhibition, matching the Breuer single-knockout phenotype. The next step is per-compound published-MIC lookup against Mycoplasma species (notebooks/toxicity_path_e_mic_lookup.ipynb, Colab) to compare predicted-toxic concentration ranges against literature MIC values.
source_detail: Reproducible by inspecting cell_sim/data/Minimal_Cell_ComplexFormation/input_data/Syn3A_updated.xml + cell_sim/data/Minimal_Cell_ComplexFormation/input_data/syn3A.gb against the v15 prediction CSV (outputs/predictions_parallel_s0.05_t0.5_seed42_thr0.1_w4_composed_all455_v15_round2_priors.csv). Output: outputs/toxicity/path_e_targets.csv (6 rows). The drug-target enzyme list was identified via gene-name + product-description regex against documented antibiotic targets in primary literature (Mupirocin: Hughes 1980 Antibiot; tavaborole / GSK2251052: Hernandez 2013 ACS Chem Biol; REP3123: Critchley 2009 J Antimicrob Chemother; auranofin: Harbut 2015 PNAS; dTMP kinase + asnRS: review-level coverage in Pohane 2018 Front Microbiol).

drug_target_enzymes.mechanism: Competitive ileRS inhibitor; freezes the enzyme in the isoleucyl-AMP-bound state
drug_target_enzymes.path_e_verdict: CONSISTENT (essential by both v15 and Breuer; saturating mupirocin predicted toxic)

drug_target_enzymes.mechanism: Bind the editing site of leuRS via a covalent enzyme-tRNA-drug adduct

drug_target_enzymes.drug_class: Phase II antibiotic for C. difficile

drug_target_enzymes.canonical_drug: TMPK-targeted nucleoside analogs (research-stage; e.g. anti-mycobacterial 5-bromo-2'-deoxyuridine 5'-monophosphate analogs)
drug_target_enzymes.mechanism: Substrate-mimetic inhibition of dTMP -> dTDP phosphorylation

drug_target_enzymes.drug_class: Repurposed FDA-approved anti-rheumatic with antibacterial activity

gate_b_correction.gate_b_claim: 0 of 155 SBML enzymes match canonical Mycoplasma-active antibiotic targets
gate_b_correction.regex_issue: Session 22's drug-target keyword search used patterns like 'isoleucyl|ileS' which missed Syn3A's 'ileRS' / 'Isoleucine--tRNA ligase' product descriptions. A broader pattern set ('isoleucine--tRNA|ileRS|Ile-tRNA') correctly identifies the canonical mupirocin target.
gate_b_correction.implication: Gate B's halt finding was over-conservative. The metabolic-only toxicity-prediction direction has 6 viable single-target case studies, not zero. The original spec's >=30 compound floor for a population-level finding is still out of reach (most compounds against these targets are research-stage with limited Mycoplasma MIC data), but case-study findings analogous to the synth-lethality 0876 x 0878 result ARE viable here.

value.next_step: notebooks/toxicity_path_e_mic_lookup.ipynb (Colab) — for each of the 6 drugs, fetch published MIC values against Mycoplasma species from ChEMBL bioactivity + PubChem BioAssay; the most concrete per-compound case study is mupirocin (well-documented MIC against M. pneumoniae and M. genitalium in clinical microbiology literature).

caveats: Path E is a SATURATING-inhibitor approximation — it treats 'compound that fully inhibits enzyme X' as equivalent to 'knockout of gene X'. This is a reasonable approximation only when (a) the compound reaches its target, (b) the inhibition is effectively complete at the dosed concentration, and (c) no off-target effects dominate. None of those is guaranteed in vivo. The approximation breaks down for partial inhibitors or compounds with poor membrane permeability — common limitations for Mycoplasma-species pharmacology because Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall but also lacks classical Gram-negative outer-membrane porins.

All six Path-E predictions are 'CONSISTENT' because the simulator already correctly calls these genes essential (they're conserved drug targets, well-annotated, in the v15 detector's knowledge base via the AnnotationClass priors). This means Path E does NOT independently corroborate the simulator — it just confirms the simulator's existing single-knockout calls translate correctly under the saturating-inhibitor model. The interesting next step (the Colab MIC lookup) is whether the predicted-toxic concentration ranges actually match published Mycoplasma MICs.

The Gate B halt fact (synthlet_gate_b_halted_negative_finding.json) remains the contemporaneous record of Session 22's decision-making and is preserved verbatim. The current fact (toxicity_path_e_saturating_inhibitor_v0) supersedes Gate B's '0/155' headline by surfacing the regex issue, but does NOT delete or modify Gate B — that would be revisionism. Both facts are valid: Gate B was honestly recorded given its inputs; Path E corrects the input set.

The 6 listed drug-target enzymes are NOT the complete set of Syn3A drug targets — they are the metabolic-network subset that's in the SBML. Outside the SBML (e.g. ribosomal proteins for macrolides/tetracyclines, DNA gyrase for fluoroquinolones, RNA polymerase for rifamycins), more drug targets exist in Layer 1-2 territory. Extending Path E to those targets requires the Layer 2 work that the original toxicity spec proposed (Path B, 3-6 weeks FTE).

Mycoplasma-specific MIC data is patchy in public databases. Mupirocin and auranofin are well-studied; REP3123, tavaborole, tirandamycin, and TMPK-targeted nucleoside analogs have limited Mycoplasma data. The Colab MIC lookup notebook is expected to return concrete numbers for 2-3 of the 6 compounds, not all six. That's a substantial fraction but not population-level coverage.

JCVISYN3A_0065 (trxA, thioredoxin) is Breuer-essential but v15 calls it non-essential (one of the 96 FNs). It is NOT included in the Path E target list because the v15-essential constraint isn't met. If the v15 detector were corrected to include trxA (e.g. via a thioredoxin annotation prior in v16), that would add a 7th drug target with auranofin as the inhibitor.
